one_liner: The reference OpenPGP command-line tool; in 2021 runs it streamed public-key encryption 1.3-2.7x faster than Sequoia's sq.
what_it_does: gpg encrypts, signs, verifies and decrypts OpenPGP messages and manages keys, with gpg-agent holding secret keys and gpgsm doing S/MIME. It is a set of executables, not a library: applications drive it through the LGPL GPGME library or the --status-fd machine interface, and all bulk cryptography is delegated to libgcrypt. The benchmarked operation is streaming encryption to one recipient (gpg -e -r KEY), compared with sq encrypt --recipient-cert.
how_it_is_fast: Data moves through a chain of iobuf filters (compression, cipher, armor) with 64 KiB default buffers, so a 10 MB encryption takes 2906 write and 2471 read syscalls where 2021 sq made 436918 writes in armor mode. Bulk crypto runs in libgcrypt's assembly (AES-NI, VAES AVX2/AVX-512 and ARMv8-CE AES, SHA-NI SHA-1, PCLMUL CRC24 for the armor checksum). Recent releases add a memcpy-free AEAD path (AES256.OCB encryption 2.2 to 4.2 GB/s on a Ryzen 5800X, commit 99e2c178c7) and skip redundant hash contexts during MDC decryption (about 3.4x faster, commit ab177eed51). Without AEAD, gpg uses CFB plus a SHA-1 MDC, and CFB encryption is inherently serial: libgcrypt has bulk VAES paths only for CFB decryption, CTR, CBC decryption, OCB, XTS and ECB.
when_to_use: Encrypting or decrypting large files or streams in shell pipelines and backups where OpenPGP is the required format and the other side runs GnuPG.
Recipients whose keys advertise the AEAD feature, so gpg 2.3+ picks OCB; GnuPG's own commit message reports 4.2 GB/s AES256.OCB encryption against 783 MB/s for AES256.CFB on the same Ryzen 5800X.

Large keyrings where key listing and lookup speed matter: with keyboxd (SQLite) gpg 2.4.5 listed 9010 keys 4.9-8.1x faster than the Sequoia gpg-sq chameleon 0.9.0 in a 2024 hyperfine report (sequoia-chameleon-gnupg issue 83), though Sequoia attributes most of the gap to uncached trust evaluation.
Smartcard, gpg-agent, ssh-agent or S/MIME workflows that need one mature, widely packaged toolchain.
when_not_to_use: Embedding OpenPGP inside a program: gpg is a process to spawn and parse (via GPGME), not an in-process library, and it is GPL-3.0-or-later, so its code cannot be copied into permissive projects.
Decryption throughput: the same 2021 thread shows sq 9.264 s vs gpg 10.944 s on a 3 GB binary message once Sequoia fixed its buffering and switched to XXH3 body hashing, so GnuPG is not faster there.

Interoperability with RFC 9580 implementations: gpg's AEAD output uses its LibrePGP OCB packet (PKT_ENCRYPTED_OCB); SEIPDv2 is emitted only with RFC-9980 keys in the --allow-9980 mode added in 2.5.23, so OCB messages may not be readable by RFC 9580 tools.
When you need fast bulk encryption to recipients without the AEAD feature flag: CFB+MDC encryption cannot be parallelized and is several times slower than OCB.

integration.form: module (command-line executables gpg, gpg-agent, gpgsm and others; programmatic use through the separate LGPL GPGME library or --status-fd)
integration.dependencies: libgpg-error 1.56+, libgcrypt 1.12.0+, libassuan 3.0.0+, libksba 1.6.3+, npth 1.2+; optional ntbtls 0.2.0+ or GnuTLS 3.2+, SQLite 3.27+ (keyboxd), zlib/bzip2; Pinentry at runtime for passphrases
integration.min_toolchain: Autotools build (configure; make) with a C99 compiler; not further documented in the README
integration.platforms: Unix-like systems and Windows (installer build documented in doc/HACKING); bulk-crypto acceleration comes from libgcrypt on x86-64 (AES-NI, VAES, SHA-NI, PCLMUL) and AArch64 (ARMv8 crypto extensions)
integration.thread_safety: not applicable to the gpg process itself; concurrent gpg invocations share gpg-agent and the keyring, and GPGME documents its own threading rules (not read this session)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — reads and writes standard OpenPGP that sq also handles (CFB+MDC, SEIPDv1), but the command-line syntax differs, and gpg's default OCB output for AEAD-capable keys uses a packet RFC 9580 tools may not accept.

gotchas: The armored comparison (2.70x) mostly measures Sequoia's 2021 armor writer, not the cipher: issue 772 (closed by commit aeacd64d on 2021-11-05) shows 'sq armor' alone at 60.3 MB/s vs 'gpg --enarmor' at 126.1 MB/s through the same dd|bar pipeline, the maintainer blamed Sequoia's slow CRC24, and sq made 43 write syscalls per KB in armor mode. gpg's armor-only rate is even below its 138.7 MB/s armored-encryption rate, so the armored rows are bounded by armoring and the pipe; bar also sat after the encryptor, so armored MB/s count base64 output bytes (about 1.4 GB for 1 GiB of input).

Harness flaws in the opening post: single run per configuration, no gpg or sq version, key type, cipher or CPU, and no control run of 'dd if=/dev/urandom | bar' alone, so the pipeline's own ceiling is unknown. GnuPG's own commit ab177eed51 measured AES256.CFB encryption at 783 MB/s on a Ryzen 5800X, so the 170.7 MB/s binary figure is not a cipher-throughput ceiling for either tool.

The cleaner data point is jgoerzen's CPU-bound file run (gpg 2.2.27 with --cipher-algo AES256 vs sq 0.25.0, i5-5200U, output to /dev/null, user time 15.5 s vs 35.4 s): both used CFB+MDC, since gpg 2.2 has no OCB, but it is still one machine and 2021 versions.

Recent releases fixed memory-safety bugs (double free in import_revoke_cert in 2.5.22; an exploitable printf bug in gpgsm's --debug x509 and OOB reads in dirmngr and scd in 2.5.23); keep to current releases.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (libaegis, HiAE, Botan, Mbed TLS, intel-ipsec-mb, Crypto++) are cipher or AEAD libraries you call in-process; pick GnuPG only when you need OpenPGP-format file encryption with key management, not raw AEAD speed. Note that the Crypto++ entry itself benchmarks faster CAST5 than libgcrypt, GnuPG's crypto backend.
verified_claims_summary: In sequoia-pgp/sequoia issue 771 (2021-11-01, filed by Sequoia developer Justus Winter), piping 1 GiB from /dev/urandom through each tool to one recipient with compression off gave gpg 170.7 MB/s vs sq 128.0 MB/s binary (1.33x) and 138.7 vs 51.4 MB/s armored (2.70x), on unstated versions and hardware; a commenter's run on an Intel Core i5-5200U with AES256 forced (gpg 2.2.27 vs sq 0.25.0, 3.3 GB file) took 16.97 s vs 36.60 s (2.16x, derived from page data). Sequoia then sped up its armor encoder and, in the same thread, overtook gpg on decryption; no newer encryption comparison was found.
status_note: Actively developed by g10 Code (2.5.24 released 2026-09-23; GitHub repo is an untracked mirror of git.gnupg.org), GPL-3.0-or-later so usable as a tool but not copyable into permissive code; the speed evidence is a 2021 single-run comparison against an early Sequoia release that has since been sped up.
